title: An ideal spring: predict, vary, explain
description: A non-causal example lab about proportional relationships. Two lessons share one course module. This template requires real course, module, and reviewed source-version IDs before validation or publication. Its numerical output is a declared idealized model, not measured experimental evidence.
objectives: Predict how changing extension affects force in a stated linear model.
Distinguish a model calculation from a real measurement and recognize a limit of the model.

lessons.title: Predict the spring's response
objectives: Use force magnitude = 40 N/m × extension to make and check a prediction.

activities.title: The model we will use
activities.body: Treat the spring as ideal over extensions from 0 to 0.30 metres, with fixed stiffness k = 40 newtons per metre. The restoring-force magnitude is F = k × x, where x is extension from the relaxed length. The force acts opposite the extension; this lab displays only its nonnegative magnitude. These are declared model assumptions, not measurements of a particular spring.

activities.title: Predict before changing the input
activities.prompt: If extension doubles from 0.05 m to 0.10 m, how should the force magnitude change under this model? Explain the relationship before using the experiment.

activities.title: Calculate one point
activities.body: At x = 0.10 m, the model gives F = 40 N/m × 0.10 m = 4 N. Metres cancel, leaving newtons. This is a model output. A measured force of 4 N would be a separate observation obtained from an actual experiment.

activities.title: Vary extension
activities.description: Hold stiffness fixed at 40 N/m and vary extension. Compare the output at 0.05, 0.10, and 0.20 m. Explain whether your prediction matched the declared model. The platform computes an affine weighted sum; it does not execute a physics engine or collect physical measurements.

activities.title: Explain the pattern
activities.prompt: State the relationship between extension and force using both words and units. What did varying the input demonstrate about this model, and what did it leave untested about a real spring?

lessons.title: Decide when the model is useful
objectives: Propose a measurement that could reveal a limit of the proportional model.

activities.title: A model has a range of use
activities.body: A real spring may approximately follow a proportional force-extension relationship only over a suitable range. Measurement noise, a force offset, and systematic curvature are different possible explanations for disagreement with a simple model. A slider that always computes 40 × x cannot test which explanation describes a physical spring.

activities.title: Interpret a hypothetical discrepancy
activities.prompt: Imagine a future measurement gives approximately 4 N at 0.10 m but 10 N at 0.20 m. Would both values fit the stated fixed-stiffness model exactly? Describe one possible explanation and one further measurement that would help investigate it. These numbers are hypothetical, not observations collected by this lab.

activities.title: Design the next check
activities.prompt: Propose a small set of extension and force measurements to compare with the model. Explain how repeated measurements or a wider set of extensions could help distinguish random noise from a systematic mismatch. State what conclusion the proposed evidence would and would not support.
